name: Maelzel’s metronome
attribution: Johann Nepomuk Maelzel
dimensions: H.: 28 cm (11.02 in.); Base: 7.1 cm (2.8.in.) square; (bottom); Base: 9.1 cm (3.6 in.) tall
evidence: The catalogue gives 28 cm high and lists mahogany, tulipwood and brass. The metronome offers a regular beat.
stake: Use a repeatable beat before sending a cue to someone who checks the gaps.
walk: Eren checks the gap against the work bell, then tries a second swing.
house: Hari places three onset marks with their gaps beside the cue words.
altText: A narrow wooden metronome case with an upright pendulum.

name: Accordion from Russia
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
dimensions: Depth: 5 cm, Width (closed): 9.5 cm (3-3/4 in.), Height: 18.5 cm (7-3/8 in.)
evidence: The catalogue gives an 1870–80 range and a closed width of 9.5 cm.
stake: Give a sound cue room on the cart without treating the closed case as a record of a playing position.
walk: Eren marks a cart space and leaves an opening mark where the clerk can see it.
house: Hari puts the closed view and a separate cue timing strip on different lines.
altText: A compact dark accordion with brass-coloured buttons.

name: Colbrun’s flutina
attribution: Frank Colbrun
medium: Rosewood, poplar, mother-of-pearl, brass, paper, leather
evidence: The 1875 accordion bears Frank Colbrun’s name on its record. The catalogue qualifies the place as possibly Belgium.
stake: Carry the maker’s name without letting a quick cue turn the tentative place into a known one.
walk: Eren keeps the place qualifier close to the short cue strip on the walk.
house: Hari gives the tentative place its own labelled edge next to the cue marks.
altText: A slender accordion with decorated sides and a rectangular keyboard section.

name: Glass harmonica attributed to Germany
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
dimensions: 117cm x 44cm x 92cm (and bits, boxes of glass)
evidence: The 18th-century record lists wood, glass and assorted material, with several loose glass components.
stake: A reader sees a run of marks on the case. Find out which events actually reach a listener.
walk: Eren keeps all three cue marks on the rail where the cart would cover one.
house: Hari separates the pattern of parts in the museum view from the marks in the fictional score.
altText: A glass harmonica case mounted on an open stand.

name: Debain’s reed organ
attribution: Alexander-François Debain
evidence: The catalogue identifies Alexander-François Debain, palisander wood and brass, and a height of 67 cm.
stake: Check which move a reader can follow while the organ profile hides part of the cue line.
walk: Eren moves the cue marks to the path side, with the source number on the edge.
house: Hari leaves the profile on a separate leaf and moves the cue times onto a clear line.
altText: A wooden reed organ with a long body raised above a stand.

name: Ch. Weiss harmonica
attribution: Ch. Weiss
evidence: The museum records this wood-and-metal harmonica as about 1895, with a length of 121 mm.
stake: A reader thinks the two harmonica pictures are the same width in the collection. Keep a timing strip and a scale separate.
walk: Eren writes 121 mm by the source number and uses the workshop cue marks to call the next turn.
house: Hari puts a scaled image key beside the timed cue so the picture width will not stand in for a duration.
altText: A metal-faced mouth organ with an embossed surface.

name: Small harmonica from Germany
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
evidence: The wood-and-metal harmonica measures 5.7 cm long. The museum dates it about 1900.
stake: A larger picture makes the smaller object easy to see. Keep the size and the cue timing attached to their proper references.
walk: Eren puts a short ruler mark on the object slip and keeps the cue beats apart.
house: Hari gives the tiny case a larger photograph space while the times keep their own ruler.
altText: A short rectangular mouth organ with a pale front.

name: Nail violin
origin: Germany, France or Bohemia in the museum record
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
dimensions: Diamter 30.2 cm. Total H. 17.3 cm Height of body 5.1 cm
evidence: The catalogue gives a 30.2 cm diameter and dates the wood-and-metal piece after about 1780. It classifies the instrument as a friction idiophone.
stake: An attendant has taken “violin” to be a name for the only way of making a sound. The guide needs a precise label before the cue travels.
walk: Eren puts the friction tag below the instrument name and above the cue times.
house: Hari keeps the museum class in view when the stage crew uses the generic signal strip.
altText: Metal nails form a ring around a round wooden soundboard.

name: Ch. Michel’s Savart-model violin
attribution: Ch. Michel
dimensions: Total length: 605 mm Body length: 352 mm
evidence: The museum records a length of 605 mm and dates Ch. Michel’s wooden violin to about 1819. It has a triangular-looking body in the collection photograph.
stake: A triangular outline is easy to recognise. Make sure the drawing and the cue each keep their own job.
walk: Eren pins a shape marker beside the fixed cue station with the accession in reach.
house: Hari separates the body-outline and measured cue intervals on the display.
altText: A violin with a triangular orange-brown body.

name: Chanot-model violin
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
dimensions: Total Length: 58.9 cm (23.0 in.) Body Length: 37.0 cm (14.5 in.) Width of upper bout:16.9 cm (7.0 in.) Width of middle bout: 11.2 cm (4.5 in.) Width lower bout: 21.4 cm (8.5 in) Rib Height. 3.1 cm (1.25 in.) Neck Length: 13.5 cm (5.37 in.) Pegbox and head Length: 9.6 cm (3.75 in.) String L. approx. 33.0 cm (12.87 in.)
evidence: The wooden violin measures 58.9 cm overall and the catalogue calls it a Chanot model.
stake: A profile can identify a style for a reader. The attendant needs another source for actual sound.
walk: Eren clips the model name next to the 58.9 cm record and supplies the workshop’s own cue.
house: Hari saves a separate model tab and leaves space for a later documented sound source.
altText: A wooden violin with a smoothly rounded outline.

name: Charles Francis Albert’s mute violin
attribution: Charles Francis Albert, Sr.
medium: Maple, ebony, brass, various other materials
dimensions: L. of body 35.7-35.9 cm (14-1/16 - 14-1/8 in); L. Overall 60.8 cm (23-15/16 in); Max. Width 19.2 cm (7-9/16 in) lower bouts
evidence: The catalogue calls this a mute violin by Charles Francis Albert, Sr., about 1886. Its overall length is 60.8 cm.
stake: A programme clerk has turned the term “mute” into a promise of silence. Try what actually arrives at the listener in the workshop.
walk: Eren labels the workshop cue with the approach that was tested and keeps a visible line for the cart pass.
house: Hari retains the object name and attaches the tested cue to its own source strip.
altText: A long-necked violin with an open, narrow body frame.

name: Rarámuri raberi
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
dimensions: L. 61 cm (24 in.); Diam. 24.1 cm (9-1/2 in.) (L. C. says, "Width, 10 in.")
evidence: The late nineteenth-century folk violin uses yellow pine and horsehair. The Met gives 61 cm as its length.
stake: A handover needs to keep the maker community with the label when the cue marks leave the stand.
walk: Eren secures the Rarámuri attribution to the numbered reference before hanging the local cue.
house: Hari leaves room for the catalogue’s instrument name and attribution above the fictional score.
altText: A pale wooden fiddle and its bow, shown together.

name: Violin from New Ireland
origin: New Ireland, Bismarck Archipelago, Papua New Guinea
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
evidence: The museum records the wooden violin at 61 cm long and separately gives 58.4 cm for the bow.
stake: The wrong dimension got clipped to the work sheet. Keep the two parts readable before adding a cue.
walk: Eren uses two short dimension labels at the near rail, then places the cue marks below them.
house: Hari puts the instrument and bow measures on separate parts of the programme.
altText: A wooden violin with a bow displayed below it.

name: Wooden violin from Texcoco
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
evidence: The late nineteenth-century record measures 48.3 × 12.7 cm and lists wood.
stake: People call several models “the wooden violin”. Keep this exact one by its own timing sheet.
walk: Eren files the Texcoco slip behind its source number and tries the cue at the low rail.
house: Hari makes the Texcoco label and the workshop cue legible from the side table.
altText: A slender orange-brown violin with a bow below.

name: Mandolin with a tentative place
origin: United States or Brazil in the museum record
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
dimensions: L. 72.4 cm (28-1/2 in.) Greatest width 28.2 cm(11-1/16 in.) Greatest depth 13.6 cm (5-5/16 in.) string length 44 cm (17-5/16 in.)
evidence: The museum gives alternative places of origin and records 72.4 cm overall, with a 44 cm string length.
stake: Two people want to call out one place. Keep both possible origins in sight through the sound trial.
walk: Eren lets both place lines travel and uses a visible mark for the beat covered by work.
house: Hari leaves the place field open to both attributions and puts the intervals next to the original working cue.
altText: A pear-shaped wooden mandolin with a long neck.

name: Mandolin with an armadillo-shell body
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
evidence: The museum lists armadillo shell, wood and gut strings and records a 74 cm length.
stake: A shell shape can help a handler name an object. A second kind of evidence is needed for what reaches a listener.
walk: Eren keeps the material wording with the accession and clears a space for the local cue.
house: Hari attaches the material note to the still view and keeps the measured beat strip free to follow.
altText: A mandolin with a curved body and a dark fingerboard.

name: Pipa by Jiu-cheng
attribution: Jiu-cheng
evidence: The record names Jiu-cheng and measures the nineteenth-century pipa at 94.2 cm long. It lists wood, ivory, bone and gut.
stake: Keep a maker’s name and the material lines readable when a reader leaves with a cue strip.
walk: Eren gives the maker’s name a full line, then gives the workshop cue its own place.
house: Hari keeps the name and materials under the catalogue number and puts the cue on the outer leaf.
altText: A tall pear-bodied pipa with strings and frets.

name: Shamisen by Isohachi Shigemoto
attribution: Isohachi Shigemoto
evidence: The catalogue names Isohachi Shigemoto, dates the instrument about 1875, and gives 96 × 19.9 × 9.3 cm.
stake: The first notice shortened the reference to one general name. Preserve the identity while the reader tries another way to follow the cue.
walk: Eren keeps a full maker line alongside the cue, with a visible mark for the covered slot.
house: Hari retains the maker on each index leaf before putting the rehearsed signal into the programme.
altText: A slender-necked shamisen with a pale square body.

name: Miniature koto
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
evidence: The museum calls this a miniature and gives its body a 49.5 cm length. The width varies along the body.
stake: A scale model can give someone a working idea of position. It needs its own source boundary before a visitor uses a sound cue beside it.
walk: Eren keeps “miniature” beside the visible signs for the local timing test.
house: Hari pairs a width note and a separate timed strip so neither size nor timing is altered by the display.
altText: A long, low miniature zither with its loose parts beside it.

name: Sanxian from China
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
evidence: The record gives 92.7 cm overall and lists rosewood, reptile skin and assorted materials.
stake: A change in a material caption should not silently change the workshop’s three original timing marks.
walk: Eren secures the new material tab at the rail and tries the same timed cue with the cart.
house: Hari keeps the support separate from the three rehearsal marks so either can be checked.
altText: A long-necked instrument with a small round body.

name: Mid-nineteenth-century wooden sitar
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
evidence: The museum measures this wooden sitar at 135.9 × 37.6 × 8.9 cm.
stake: The thin side profile rarely shows the overall length well. The stage needs the intended reference and a readable cue.
walk: Eren clips an overall length arrow to the image key and puts the cue timing on another line.
house: Hari makes space for an end-view heading with the source and keeps the timing marks prominent beside it.
altText: A long-necked sitar with a bulbous orange-brown body.

name: Gumbeng tube zither
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
evidence: The catalogue distinguishes an approximate 81.1 cm total length from the approximately 60.2 cm tube.
stake: The hire desk combined lengths and lost the boundary between the whole and the tube. Keep that boundary beside a tested cue.
walk: Eren marks “whole” and “tube” on two lines, then tests the near-rail signal.
house: Hari gives each extent its own heading on the object copy. A different line records when to start the fictional signal.
altText: Two views of a narrow bamboo tube instrument with projecting ends.

name: Suling pélog from Sunda
origin: Sunda, Indonesia in the museum record
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
evidence: The museum lists bamboo and rattan and measures the ring flute at 50.7 × 1.6 cm.
stake: A slim object drawing can catch a reader’s eye. It needs a separate record before anyone treats it as evidence of a particular sound.
walk: Eren leaves a readable heading for the flute reference and marks all three fictional cues on the rail.
house: Hari puts the pictured flute and the workshop’s audible timing trial above two separate captions.
altText: A long slim orange-brown bamboo ring flute.

name: Ipu hokiokio from Hawaiʻi
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
evidence: The gourd nose flute is 6.2 cm long and 4.5 cm at its maximum diameter, according to the catalogue.
stake: The draft calls the biggest view the biggest object. Separate the object scale from the usable visibility of the cue.
walk: Eren gives the visible line room for all three cue marks and keeps the stated dimensions by the drawing.
house: Hari puts the small gourd’s dimensions by the image and lets the reader keep the cue timeline at a larger size.
altText: A small rounded gourd instrument with round openings.

name: Puniu from Hawaiʻi
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
evidence: The museum lists coconut shell, fish skin and fibre. The 19th-century record gives 10.8 cm in height and 11.4 cm in diameter.
stake: Different parts are visible from above or the side. The cue needs to reach a listener who works from the side.
walk: Eren keeps height and diameter labels on separate edges of the guide and puts cue marks at the rail.
house: Hari preserves the two dimension headings and moves the fictional timings to a line that can be read seated.
altText: A small round reddish drum with a dark drumhead.

name: Reed pipe from Fiji
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
dimensions: L. 10 in., Diam. shell 3 in. (L.C. says, "L. 11 in.")
evidence: The catalogue measures the shell at 3 inches across. Its length line gives 10 inches and records a separate note saying 11 inches.
stake: An earlier copy hid the second length. Keep both entries available while planning the local reader’s signal.
walk: Eren clips both catalogue lengths beside the source number and uses the tests to choose a cue line.
house: Hari keeps the two unequal figures visible in the source pocket and puts the common timings underneath.
altText: A reed pipe with a long shaft and bound shell section.

name: Gore notched flute from Aoba
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
dimensions: L. 24 7/8 × Diam. 1 1/16 in. (63.2 × 2.7 cm) Additional measurements in mm: overall length 632; to holes: 450, 557 (front), 613 (back); round notch 8; maximum diameter: inside 23, outside 27
evidence: The museum describes a bamboo flute 63.2 cm long with a 2.7 cm diameter.
stake: This exact flute needs its home and size visible. Keep the fictional reader’s timing problem distinct from possible relatives in the catalogue.
walk: Eren writes the Aoba heading above the record and moves the trial cue to a reachable part of the rail.
house: Hari places the source number next to the name and keeps the measured intervals in the workshop’s own box.
altText: A straight notched bamboo flute in a side view.

name: Gore notched flute attributed to Norfolk Island
origin: Norfolk Island in the museum record
attribution: Maker unrecorded in the collection entry
dimensions: L. 13-3/8 in., Diam. 3/4 in. (L. 34.2 cm, D.+/-1.5 cm --Richard Campbell, '80) L. 1-3/8 x Diam. 9/16 (interior 1/2) in. (34 x 1.5 [interior 1.2] cm.) Lehman
evidence: The museum title gives a notched flute, with a later measurement of 34.2 cm and approximate diameter of 1.5 cm.
stake: A listener has connected two records by their shared title. Preserve this catalogue’s own location and measurement before leaving a cue.
walk: Eren gives this reference its own numbered clip, then checks the audible line across the service bend.
house: Hari leaves a separate reference for the 34.2 cm measurement and writes the usable timings beside it.
altText: A slim bamboo flute with enlarged views of two sections.

name: Accordion by Alexandre Père & Fils
attribution: Alexandre Père & Fils
medium: Wood, metal, mastic, brass, tortoiseshell, gilt brass, mother-of-pearl, silver foil
evidence: The catalogue dates the instrument to 1850–55. It gives 38.5 × 13.5 × 17.5 cm when closed.
stake: A support must retain the word “closed”. The reader gives the working cue enough room on its own line.
walk: Eren leaves the closed-case measure with the object and puts a separate mark where the signal restarts.
house: Hari puts “closed” next to the numbers and gives the cue a second line with clear first and last marks.
altText: A tall dark accordion with floral ornament along its side.

name: Tintype of a woman holding an accordion
origin: United States in the museum catalogue
attribution: Photographer and sitter unnamed in the collection entry
evidence: The late 1860s photograph measures 9.2 by 6.5 cm. The catalogue identifies the held instrument as an accordion.
stake: A guest wants to know what she was playing. Leave the photographed pose and the workshop’s test cue on separate lines.
walk: Eren leaves the picture source and a note about the held accordion. The local cue has a clear line of its own.
house: Hari files the photographed moment with its date and keeps the tested signal outside the image frame.
altText: A tintype portrait of a seated woman holding an accordion.
